title: The Hollywood Mythical Odyssey Movie
author: Evaggelos Vallianatos
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/word-
image-419421-1-scaled.jpeg)

Odysseus and the Sirens by John William Waterhouse, 1891. National Gallery of
Victoria, Melbourne, Australia. Wikipedia, Public Domain.

**Prologue**

[Christopher Nolan](https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-
arts/movies/story/2026-07-07/christopher-nolan-explains-how-he-made-the-
odyssey-
interview?sfmc_id=6532a75f25b3640666d1eccb&utm_id=46480312&skey_id=f6cfc7ff765383351b8403a238de73bdd488d7c0e9bdfc61f6cfd132f9d568e8&utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ALERT-
Email-List-
Exclusive:%20Christopher%20Nolan%20explains%20‘The%20Odyssey’-20260707&utm_term=Alert%20-%20Sub%20and%20Nonsub%20minus%20Entertainment),
producer of “The Odyssey” movie, admitted he was enchanted from childhood by
Homer’s Odyssey. He produced a 250-million dollars film that rewrites both
Homer’s Odyssey and Greek history. His Odyssey movie separates the Greeks from
their gods. However, Greeks and their gods were inseparable.

**The Greeks and their gods**

“Told in this way, with divine intervention at a minimum,” says [Richard
Brady](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/07/27/the-odyssey-christopher-
nolan-movie-review?_sp=caf3bbf2-f6a3-4a33-b0e6-93f364447fa9.1784223156738) of
the New Yorker, “the story remains an exciting adventure filled with passion,
terror, tenderness, and wonder, but it lacks the particular thrill that comes
with reading Homer, a sense of the gulf that separates modern minds from
Bronze Age ones…. By suppressing this continuity between the natural and the
supernatural realms, Nolan omits much of what makes the Homeric age so
different, including the ambience of the divine and the distinctive moral
realm that goes with it…. rather than trying to take the audience inside the
ancient Greek mind-set, Nolan chooses a slimmed-down, almost naturalistic
approach, tamed and tempered…. Psychologizing Odysseus… lends “The Odyssey” a
readily digestible modernity—ancient Greeks, they’re just like us!—but does so
at the expense of the richness of detail and the societal complexity that
makes reading Homer such a vital and immediate experience.”

Beautifully said. I fully agree with Brady.

Nolan feels uncomfortable with the Greek gods. His reading of Homer has the
monotheistic fear of the gods being so close to the Greeks, thus missing the
subtlety and beauty of the Homeric poetry and story of the enormous energy,
passion and struggle of Odysseus to return home to Ithaca.

Homer starts the Odyssey with an assembly of the gods to decide the return of
Odysseus to Ithaca. Both Zeus and his daughter Athena like Odysseus and agree
they should restrain Poseidon from killing him because Odysseus blinded
Cyclops Polyphemos, son of Poseidon. Athena is close to Odysseus. Without her
insights and advice, there would have not been an Odyssey. None of these
connections are obvious in Nolan’s Odyssey.

**Nostos, day of return**

Nolan misses completely the real purpose of the Odyssey, that is, the dramatic
effort of Odysseus to return home to his wife Penelope and son Telemachos. The
exciting and passionate day of return, the Homeric νόστιμον ήμαρ, is absent
from “The Odyssey” movie of Nolan.

**History of Homer and the Trojan War**

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/word-
image-419421-2-scaled.jpeg)

Astronomical phenomena during the Trojan War. Homer describes a solar eclipse
in the Odyssey 20.356-357. On the left, we see the killing of Patroklos by
Hektor, and on the right, the killing of Hektor by Achilles as well as the
killing of the suitors by Odysseus. Painting by Evi Sarantea.

The other problematic aspect of Nolan’s film is that Nolan, like most modern
students of Homer, assumes wrongly that the Trojan War was made up, that it
was not a historical event.

Homer existed (Anthologia Palatina 14.102) and the Trojan War happened in late
13th or early 12th century BCE. Two teams of
[astronomers](https://www.counterpunch.org/2025/07/29/minoan-gate-of-heavens-
and-earth/) confirmed the eclipses of the Sun that Homer described in his
Odyssey (20.356-357). Just as fundamental in establishing the historical
origins of the Odyssey, is the evidence from Aristotle. He was the greatest
philosopher of all time. He was the inventor of zoology and meteorology in the
4th century BCE. Aristotle loved Homer and repeatedly cited him in his
philosophical, scientific and political works. Aristotle trusted Homer, the
teacher of the Greeks for centuries. His epics were Greek language, myth,
history, astronomy, cosmology, science and technology, geography, traditions,
piety for the gods and pride for Greek civilization. Greeks read, sang, copied
and gained inspiration from Homer. Aristotle edited Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey
for his pupil, Alexander the Great. He would not have tolerated falsehoods and
fiction from anyone, much less Homer.

In modern times, and especially in 21st century America, not merely Homer but
all Greeks cause anxiety to theologians, scholars and theater and movie
producers. [Daniel
Mendelsohn](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/10/opinion/odyssey-movie-lupita-
nyongo-nolan.html), who translated the Odyssey, liked the Nolan film of the
Odyssey. He says that “Helen of Troy is starting wars again. But this time the
legendarily beautiful, semi-divine queen of myth, whose adulterous elopement
with the Trojan prince Paris brought on the 10-year-long Trojan War, has
launched a thousand tweets.”

All this may be partly true about beautiful Helen, but she was not fictional.
She was the daughter of Zeus and the queen of Sparta that eloped with Paris or
Paris abducted her. And, yes, she caused wars then and slight controversy now.

Mendelsohn explains that Helen was “a skilled orator and the object of
skillful oratory.” True. Helen in Nolan’s account is neither beautiful nor
eloquent. She is insignificant. But the timeliness of Nolan’s film was not
accidental. American politics, Trump in the White House, the war Trump and
Netanyahu of Israel have been fighting against ancient Persia / Iran at a time
when the US is a badly divided society and in dramatic decline might have
something to do with Nolan’s choices. Still, Nolan’s Odyssey is not completely
divorced from Homer.

**Is Nolan asking us to dream bigger?**

A reviewer, in fact, raises Nolan to heavens. “Nolan’s love of movies and
commitment to them — to what they can do, what they can be, what they should
be -" says Manohla Dargis, chief film critic of the New York Times, “runs like
an electric current through his filmography, lighting it, and oftentimes you,
up. That passion is in every frame of his [monumental adaptation of “The
Odyssey](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/15/movies/the-odyssey-review.html),”
one of the most Nolan of Nolan spectacles in its thematic concerns, formal
playfulness, kinetic thrills and unabashed showmanship…. he always aims to
please…. Nolan turns a mythological tale into cinematic realism with creaking
wood and straining rope, the grunts and cries of men. He brings characters who
can seem exotically distant nearer to us, humanizing people, including those
Odysseus will soon help slaughter…. Nolan asks us to dream bigger. His
“Odyssey” is a classic in every sense, a transporting affirmation of the art
and a work of pure cinema.”

This extraordinary praise is mostly fiction. Dargis is under the delusion she
is reviewing a story of myth, in which case exaggeration causes little harm.
But as I have already explained, the Odyssey is a real icon of the struggle to
return home of a very intelligent, god-like Odysseus. Goddess Athena loved
him. Nolan is in no position to “humanize” the Greeks. On the contrary, “The
Odyssey” humanizes us. And Nolan is not asking us to dream bigger. In fact,
the thunderous noise and ear-piercing sounds, lightnings, and violence crushes
our dreams. We are tempted to think we see a new super big science fiction
story.

**The Odyssey movie**

I went and saw “The Odyssey” movie. Nolan excels in depicting warfare, fear,
terror and danger. For example, he captures the terror of the crossing of the
strait of Messina between Sicily and Calabria in southern Italy by Odysseus
and his crew. We could see the wind-powered Bronze Age ships of Odysseus
headed straight for the dangerous giant round blue whirlwind waters of
Charybdis. And those who survived Charybdis were attacked by the six-headed
monsters of black Skylla, female dogs. Those monsters grabbed some of the crew
of Odysseus for eating them.

Nolan did what he pleased with the text and stories of the Homeric Odyssey. In
each episode he brought to life, he added or subtracted characters or details
of what Homer described. He ignored Aiolos, god of the winds, who had put all
the winds in a leather bag, while he allowed only a Western wind that would
take Odysseus’ ships to Ithaca. Aiolos, however, warned Odysseus not to open
the wind bag. And Homer says that Aiolos’ wind drove the ships very close to
Ithaca. But despite Odysseus’ warnings to the sailors not to touch the wind
bag, while asleep, the crew opened the bag thinking Odysseus was hiding gold
in the bag. Once the winds were outside the bag, they forced the ships to
return to the Aiolos island. The heartbroken Odysseus spoke to Aiolos, but the
wind god was angry and ordered Odysseus off his island. Nothing from this
exciting episode appears in Nolan’s Odyssey.

The other distressing change Nolan did was to alter events. Once Odysseus and
his crew landed accidentally to the land of the Laestrygonians, Nolan added
more terror by converting the giant cannibals to giant mechanical robots that
killed most the followers of Odysseus. Only the ship of Odysseus and its crew
escaped the slaughter.

In the case of the Cyclops, only terror and screams and frightened sheep
running withing the semi dark large cave dominated the confrontation of the
monster one-eyed son of Poseidon eating a few of the crew of Odysseus. Homer,
however, allowed Odysseus to talk to the Cyclops and get him drunk, which gave
the trapped Greeks an opportunity to blind Polyphemos and escape his deadly
grip by tying themselves under the belly of large sheep. None of these
interactions appeared in Nolan’s film.

Nolan also modified the Homeric story of Odysseus meeting Circe, daughter of
the Sun god Helios. Nolan shows Circe as an elderly woman who metamorphosed a
number of Odysseus crew into pigs. He avoided reporting that the messenger of
the gods, god Hermes, interrupted Odysseus on his way to confront Circe.
Hermes gave Odysseus Μῶλυ, a plant / drug that cancelled the magic power of
Circe. With that divine advice and strength, Odysseus forced Circe to undo her
evil work. Nolan deleted this important affair between Hermes and Odysseus and
then Odysseus and Circe.

Nolan also bypassed the very important “visit” of Odysseus to the dream-like
island of Phaiakia / Kerkyra. The stormy sea threw the almost drowned and
naked Odysseus in a beach of Phaiakia, very close to a small number of women
washing clothes. Princess Nausicaa, daughter of King Alkinous and Queen Arete,
and her servants discovered the suffering Odysseus buried in olive tree leaves
very close to the waters of a river emptying in the Ionian sea. Odysseus
explained to Nausikaa, as well as he could, his dangerous travels. Nausikaa
assured him all was well; she found clothes for him and guided Odysseus to her
father.

King Alkinous was pleased to meet Odysseus. He feasted him in his palace.
During the festivities, Demodokos, a local bard (αοιδός) sang from the poetry
of Homer the exploits of Odysseus (Odyssey 8.46). At that moment, Odysseus
broke down. He covered his head with his cloak and started crying. Alkinous
noticed the drama and urged Odysseus and his guests to go outside for athletic
competition. Odysseus displayed his athletic Prowers. Then Alkinous asked him
to speak about himself, revealing his name and identity. Odysseus said: “I am
Odysseus, son of Laertes. I am known all over the world for my cunning. My
fame even reached the heavens. I come from the island of Ithaca.” (Odyssey
9.21-24). Odysseus then pleaded with Alkinous to help him to return home to
Ithaca. Alkinoos did. He offered a ship to carry him to Ithaca. The ship was
pilotless. It had advanced technology that read the thoughts of the
passengers. It took the sleeping Odysseus to Ithaca. When Odysseus woke up in
Ithaca, he was lost. He did not recognize Ithaca after 20 years of absence.
Goddess Athena was waiting for Odysseus in Ithaca. She told Odysseus he was at
home. She informed him of the crisis at his home with Penelope being courted
by several powerful men, proposing marriage to her. Penelope was torn between
her love for Odysseus and the marriage proposals of handsome and powerful men.
She was convinced Odysseus was dead.

While Nolan ignored this important experience of Odysseus in Phaiakia, he
highlighted the violent effort of the suitors to capture the kingdom of Ithaca
by deception and teasing of Penelope. We see Odysseus entering the fray
dressed like a beggar. Athena had also made him look like a very old man.
Odysseus enters the palace and begs for food among the suitors enjoying
themselves. They ate meat and bread and drank wine. They sat on comfortable
chairs around large wooden tables in the main hall of the palace.

The beggar Odysseus had been recognized by his faithful dog Argos and his old
nurse Eurykleia. The dog moved slowly his tail and died. Eurykleia was washing
his legs when she noticed a wound he had suffered from hunting a wild boar
when he was a teenager. Odysseus prevented her from expressing her joy.

Nolan’s movie resurrects the strategic patience of the warrior Odysseus, his
tenacity, courage and power and knowledge of the use of his old weapons, the
wooden bow and bronze-tipped arrows. We barely see details but hear the
screams and blows of men fighting to death. Odysseus kills most of the
suitors. His son Telemachos and his old shepherd Eumaios are his sole co-
warriors. At the end of the palace battle, we see the victorious Odysseus with
two arrows on his back. Nolan ends the movie with dead Odysseus, which
contradicts Homer. Odysseus lived a happy life with Penelope and Telemachos.
But with several flashbacks of Odysseus we witness extraordinary events,
including the building of the Wooden Horse and the horrific burning of Troy.

**Epilogue**

Homer was the son of Telemachos, who was the son of Odysseus and Penelope.
Homer’s mother was Polykaste, daughter of Nestor, King of Pylos who fought in
the Trojan War (Anthologia Palatina 14.102). This explains the richness of
events and details of the epic poems, Iliad and Odyssey. The Iliad tells the
story of the historical Trojan War and the Odyssey the passionate struggle of
Odysseus to return home to Ithaca.

The Trojans were Greeks, who had left mainland Greece for Ionia or Asia Minor.
Odysseus was the greatest of all heroes who fought in the Trojan War. His
Wooden Horse deception destroyed Troy and started his desperate journey to
find his way back to Ithaca.

Homer’s epics have been the foundation stones of Hellenic and Western
literature and civilization. They have no precedent, though they influenced
literature to our own time. Yet Westerners have always had great difficulties
to translate those epics into readable and accurate prose or stage them as
worthwhile theater plays or movies.

The latest effort by Christopher Nolan of Hollywood to make “The Odyssey”
movie reflects the perennial problem of helping the Western viewer feel
comfortable in reading and understanding the Greek mind. Yes, to some degree,
we are all Greeks.

Nolan took the Odyssey of Homer and made a Hollywood adventure full of
excitement, violence, thunderous sounds, terror and warfare. These
exaggerations do reflect events in the Odyssey, but they are removed from
their Greek context of ceaseless communication and relationships between
Greeks and their gods. The gods, Greeks thought, could disguise themselves as
the strangers one meets (Homer, “The Odyssey” 17.524-529). The second failure
of Nolan’s praiseworthy effort was the metaphysical and political assumptions
that Homer’s poems were imaginary. That is, neither the Iliad nor the Odyssey
represent historical events. Of course, these assumptions are wrong. Homer
existed and wrote for the most part about historical events. Finally, the
third failure of Nolan was to film this Homeric movie in the [Morocco-occupied
land of Western Sahara](https://www.democracynow.org/2026/7/17/the_odyssey).
Why did he not produce the movie in Greece? His decision to do the work in
Western Sahara has given rise to protests against the movie. The people of
Western Sahara rightly resent Western companies like Universal Pictures doing
business with Morocco, which for 50 years is occupying their country.

I hope Nolan would abandon Morocco’s Western Sahara. He ought to recreate his
Odyssey movie in Greece. In that process, the best guide is Homer. Let the
gods have their say. That way, he and the new movie will have the opportunity
to read the Greek mind and educate Americans and Western people of the
beauties and wisdom of Greek culture.
